content:
Yesterday saw two conflicting reports about next year's iPhone; the device, seen as the iPhone's twentieth-anniversary commemorative model, is also described as the concrete realisation of Apple's long-standing "a sheet of glass" vision.

As for what we can actually expect, the reports have been contradicting each other for some time, but yesterday's divergence could be called the most dramatic so far…

Current situation

Former Apple design chief Jony Ive has often spoken of his long-term vision of ultimately turning the iPhone into "a sheet of glass"; even though Ive has left the company, the mainstream view remains that Apple has been steadily moving in that direction.

Although Apple generally does not throw big celebrations for anniversaries, the consensus is that they hope to get as close as possible to realising this vision before the iPhone's twentieth anniversary. This could include embedding Face ID beneath the display and hiding the front camera under the screen.

However, we have already seen contradictory reports on these expectations. The original view was that this would be a standalone model, similar to the iPhone Air and the upcoming iPhone Ultra, but more recent reports point to the design appearing on next year's iPhone Pro models.

As for naming, it would be called the iPhone 19 Pro, but Apple could also opt to skip a generation and name it the iPhone 20 to mark the anniversary.

Yesterday's contradictory reports

When an analyst claimed Apple had abandoned plans to launch an all-glass iPhone next year, yesterday's situation became even more muddled.

But Bloomberg's Mark Gurman immediately pushed back on that claim.

The more likely scenario

The point is that Apple's vision for the iPhone does not have a single, final destination. What they plan to roll out next year is only one step—or a few steps—toward that sci-fi-inspired "a sheet of glass" vision.

The question is not whether that goal can be achieved next year, but how far Apple will move in that direction. But whether it is one step or several, this will absolutely not be the last step in the iPhone's design evolution.

In fact, Gurman revealed that Apple has in fact scaled back some of its previous expectations for next year.

Jefferies' analyst likely received the same information, just half a beat late, and mistakenly assumed the entire plan had been shelved.

My personal expectation is that next year's design will be a major leap—comparable to the breakthrough of the iPhone X—but there will be further developments in the years that follow. For me, the biggest question is whether the 2027 iPhone will have a breakthrough large enough to be marked in some special way, such as being labelled a twentieth-anniversary commemorative iPhone (which I think is unlikely), being given a special name, or skipping a generation and being called the iPhone 20.

What are your expectations? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
